title: Why parables? (Mark 4:10–20)
hook: the disciples don't get it either, and he explains the sower

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower again, told from a boat, wrapped in hearken, in listening. Your line was let anyone with ears hear. Did you listen someone all the way to the end? Day one hundred seventy-two.

You're in a class, and the teacher finishes something everyone else seems to follow. Heads nod. You have no idea what just happened. You wait until the room empties, then walk up and say, quietly, sorry, can you explain that? That's today. The crowd thins out. And when he's alone, the twelve, plus a few others who stayed, come to Jesus and ask what the sower story meant. The people closest to him, who'd left their nets and their tax booth for this, didn't get it. Mark doesn't hide that. Today: why parables?
screen: `THE CROWD GOES HOME.` → `THE TWELVE STAY BEHIND.` → `WHAT DID THAT MEAN?`

segments.voice: Jesus's first answer is a hard passage. He tells them the secret of the kingdom has been given to them, but to those outside everything comes in parables, and he uses words from the prophet Isaiah about people who look and look but don't see, and hear and hear but don't understand. It sounds as though stories are meant to keep people out. Christians don't all read it the same way. Some hear it as describing what parables do rather than what Jesus wants: a parable opens up to anyone who leans in and asks, like the twelve did, and stays shut to anyone who walks away. Others read it with Isaiah, whose message was also going to meet closed ears. Then comes the line that makes Mark so human, in the old King James Bible: "Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?" A little exasperated. A little fond. And he explains. "The sower soweth the word." The path is people who hear it, and at once it's snatched away. The rocky ground is people who take it up with joy, but have no root, and fall away when trouble comes. The thorns are "the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things." And the good ground hears, takes it in, and bears fruit. Notice what makes you an insider here. Not being clever. Asking. The ones who got the explanation were the ones who admitted, out loud, that they didn't understand. In Mark, the disciples will keep not getting it for chapters. And he keeps explaining.
screen: `TO THOSE OUTSIDE, PARABLES.` · `KNOW YE NOT THIS PARABLE?` · `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` · `THE INSIDERS WERE THE ONES WHO ASKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one thing you don't understand. Settle, and breathe. Let something come to mind that you nod along to but don't really get. A part of your faith, or someone else's. How your own money works. Why someone you love does what they do. A word at work everyone uses. Say it to yourself plainly: I don't understand this. Notice whether that feels like shame or like relief. If you pray, you can bring the question to God the way the twelve did, after the crowd left. The bell holds the time.
Why parables? The disciples' question after the crowd left, and the answer only askers got.
Your line: they didn't get it either. Today, ask one question you'd usually be too embarrassed to ask. Day one hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 172 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP ON A STAND.`

howItsDone: Many Christians study scripture in small groups where asking what a passage means is expected, and churches often teach the explanation of the sower alongside the parable itself.

fork.setup: you're one of the twelve. everyone else nodded, but you didn't understand the story at all. what do you do?
options: nod along and hope it comes to you.
wait till the crowd leaves and ask him.
ask another disciple to explain it.
fork.reveal: they asked him when they were alone, and he explained it to them. in Mark, the insiders are the ones who asked.

original.note: Greek: a throwing beside, one thing set next to another to compare. It gives English parable.

trapdoor: what you thought: parables are simple stories anyone can get.
what it means: even the twelve didn't get it. they asked, and the explanation went to the ones who asked.
what a scholar hears: Mark 4:12 echoes Isaiah 6:9–10 without naming him, a hard line that readers take in more than one way.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: Mark 4:12 uses Isaiah's words without naming Isaiah, so 'quotes the prophet Isaiah' became 'uses words from'; added a second reading of 4:11–12 as the earlier note asked; path explanation now matches 4:15 (taken away at once); cut 'one of the hardest', 'for centuries', 'many', and the invented boat detail.
Mark 4:11–12 (parables 'that seeing they may see, and not perceive') is paraphrased and presented as hard, with one common reading attributed to 'many'. Keepers may want a second reading named.
The explanation (4:14–20) is summarized; confirm the summary.
